notes.title: Chapter map: Typing & interfaces
notes.html:
Annotations do nothing at runtime: every note is either what a static checker does with them (46–49) or who reads them at runtime anyway (50–50b). Read each arrow as a sentence: protocols built on generics & variance.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH, grey = another chapter (dashed edges).

Reading order: 46 type hints ─▶ 47 generics & variance ─▶ 48 protocols ─▶ 49 ABCs ─▶ 50 introspection ─▶ 50a Pydantic ─▶ 50b structured outputs

These notes offer alternatives for one question, so a decision tree earns its place here, not in each note:

  • The one big idea: CPython stores annotations and ignores them. A checker uses them to prove the code consistent before it runs; Pydantic uses them to prove the data valid when it arrives. Neither replaces the other.
  • The two most-confused pairs: Protocol vs ABC (48 vs 49: matched by shape and checked statically vs inherited and enforced at runtime) · int | None vs int | None = None (50b: only the default decides required, which strict LLM providers care about).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: 48's structural-vs-nominal class diagram, 50a's build-once / run-many flowchart, then 50b's round-trip sequence diagram.
  • Cross-chapter: dunder protocols (the language's own structural interfaces) · dataclasses (the non-validating choice for internal data) · reliability mechanics (validation errors aren't retried; transport errors may be).

notes.title: Type Hints & typing
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 typing: support for type hints · 📘 Static typing with Python (spec) · 📜 PEP 484: type hints · 📜 PEP 649: deferred annotations · 📖 mypy type hints cheat sheet

⚡ TL;DR

The interpreter stores hints and ignores them; a static checker reads them and runs nothing. So hints catch bugs before they run, but only where a checker sees a precise type flowing all the way through.

🧭 Flow: annotate signatures ─▶ the interpreter stores them in __annotations__ (lazily on 3.14+) and checks nothing ─▶ mypy or pyright infers a type for every expression ─▶ reports each mismatch with file and line, before anything runs ─▶ libraries that opt in (pydantic, dataclasses, FastAPI) read them at runtime

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Are type hints enforced at runtime? No: stored in __annotations__, ignored by the interpreter.
Who uses them? Static checkers (mypy, pyright) and opt-in libraries (pydantic, dataclasses, FastAPI).
Any vs object? Any switches checking off; object accepts anything but allows almost nothing until narrowed.
Does Optional[X] mean the argument can be omitted? No: the value may be None; only a default makes it omittable.
What changed in 3.14? Annotations are evaluated lazily (PEP 649/749); annotationlib reads them as forward refs.
✏️ Draw by hand: the two worlds Checker lane: source → infer types → errors in CI. Runtime lane: store hints, ignore them; opt-in libraries read them.

💡 The idea

Python finds a type error only when the offending line runs. Add annotations and run the same bad call:

def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"hi {name}"
greet(42)                    # → 'hi 42'   nothing checked
greet.__annotations__        # → {'name': <class 'str'>, 'return': <class 'str'>}

The interpreter stored the hints and ignored them. The value comes from a static checker run over the code without executing it. Here is the bug hints exist to catch, a function that can return None fed into one that can't accept it:

def find_user(uid: int) -> str | None:
    return None if uid < 0 else "raje"
def shout(s: str) -> str:
    return s.upper()
shout(find_user(-1))
# $ mypy --strict users.py   (mypy 2.4.0)
# → error: Argument 1 to "shout" has incompatible type "str | None"; expected "str"  [arg-type]

At runtime the same line is an AttributeError on the one request where the user isn't found; the checker found it on every path, before anything ran.

The trade: hints cost annotation effort and a checker in CI, and in exchange every path is checked before it runs, but only by the checker, never by Python itself.

⚙️ How it works

Two separate worlds, joined only by __annotations__:

The checker never runs code and the interpreter never checks hints. The vocabulary that decides what the checker allows:

Rule What actually happens
X | None / Optional[X] The value may be None; whether the caller may omit it depends only on a default. int | None and Union[int, None] are the same typing.Union object on 3.14.
Any vs object Any disables checking: mypy accepted a.whatever() on Any and rejected it on object ("object" has no attribute "whatever").
Narrowing After if x is not None: or isinstance(x, str), the checker treats x as the narrower type in that branch; reveal_type(expr) prints what it thinks.
Gradual typing Unannotated code is Any, so checkers stay quiet about it by default; --strict turns untyped defs, implicit Any and stale ignores into errors.
Lazy annotations (3.14, PEP 649/749) def later(x: Undefined) raised NameError at definition on 3.12; on 3.14 it defined fine and raised only when __annotations__ was read.

💻 Code

The configuration that turns hints into a real safety net, rolled out package by package:

[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.12"
strict = true                       # untyped defs, implicit Optional, Any leaks are errors
warn_unused_ignores = true          # a stale `# type: ignore` is itself an error
plugins = ["pydantic.mypy"]         # understands BaseModel fields

[[tool.mypy.overrides]]             # gradual: strict for new code, lenient for legacy
module = ["legacy.*", "scripts.*"]
disallow_untyped_defs = false
check_untyped_defs = true           # still check the bodies we can

[[tool.mypy.overrides]]
module = ["some_untyped_sdk.*"]     # no stubs: contain it, don't ignore globally
ignore_missing_imports = true

strict stops untyped functions silently returning Any into typed code; the overrides make adoption incremental. Run it in CI as a required check, or hints decay into comments.

⚠️ Break it: the interpreter and the checker disagree about the same file.

def add_tax(amount: float, rate: float) -> float:
    return amount * (1 + rate)
print(add_tax("100", 0.2))           # a str where a float is declared
# look for: Python raises inside the function, not at the call; mypy flags the call
# naive model predicts: Python raises "amount must be float" at the call

python fails with TypeError: can't multiply sequence by non-int of type 'float' on the multiplication inside add_tax; with rate=2 it silently prints 100100100. mypy reports Argument 1 to "add_tax" has incompatible type "str"; expected "float" without running anything.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: No, hints aren't enforced at runtime. The interpreter stores them in __annotations__ and ignores them, so greet(42) against name: str just runs. A static checker, mypy or pyright, reads the source and reports inconsistencies in the editor and CI. A few libraries read them on purpose: pydantic validates from them, dataclasses generate __init__, FastAPI builds request parsing. On 3.14 they're evaluated lazily.

Q · Mechanism — Optional[X] versus a default argument; X | Y versus Union[X, Y]? Optional[X] is exactly X | None: may be None. A default is what makes an argument omittable: def f(x: int | None) requires it but allows None; def f(x: int = 0) allows omitting it but not None; def f(x: int | None = None) allows both (current mypy no longer infers Optional from a None default). X | Y is the 3.10+ spelling of Union[X, Y]; checkers treat them identically and on 3.14 they're the same runtime object.

Q · Failure — Hints everywhere, yet None reaches code expecting a str. How, and what catches it? Any leaks: an untyped function, a library without stubs, json.loads, a dict[str, Any] config, cast or a # type: ignore, and Any is assignable to str. External data is never checked statically. Catch it with a required strict checker in CI for the service's code, and a pydantic validation boundary where untyped data enters, so None fails at the edge instead of three layers in.

Q · Design — Add real typing to a 200,000-line untyped service without a big-bang rewrite. Get a checker into CI at zero new errors first: lenient mode, the existing errors recorded as a baseline, CI failing only on regressions. Turn on check_untyped_defs, then ratchet package by package: each package at zero errors moves into a strict override, and new code is strict from day one. Add stub packages and local stubs for dependencies. I'd watch decay first: a CI report of strict coverage per package that fails on a rising ignore count.

⚖️ Compare

Annotation Means Checker allows Runtime effect
x: int an int int operations none
x: int | None int or None nothing int-specific until narrowed none
x: int = 0 int, may be omitted int operations the default applies
x: Any checking off everything none
x: object any value almost nothing until narrowed none
cast(int, x) "trust me" treats x as int returns x unchanged

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Type hints make Python check types"
    ✅ The interpreter ignores them (see Break it).
    ↳ Fix: a required checker in CI, plus runtime validation at the edges.
  • 🪞 "Optional[str] means the parameter is optional"
    ✅ It means the value may be None; only a default makes it omittable.
  • ❌ "Fully typed code can't ship type errors"
    ✅ Any, json.loads, cast and # type: ignore all bypass checking.
    ↳ Fix: strict mode, warn_unused_ignores, and a validation boundary.
  • 🔀 Not the same as runtime validation
    ↳ Difference: a checker proves your code is consistent; it can't prove data from HTTP, JSON or an LLM matches.
    ↳ So: validate at the boundary with pydantic.
  • ⚠️ Don't paper over errors with Any, cast or # type: ignore.
    ↳ Why: each is a hole the checker can't see through.
    ↳ Instead: narrow, add stubs, or fix the type; review ignores like code.
  • ⚠️ Don't adopt strict mode for a whole legacy codebase at once.
    ↳ Why: a check that fails on day one gets disabled.
    ↳ Instead: baseline, then ratchet package by package.

How annotations have changed (behaviour checked on CPython 3.12.13 and 3.14.6, mypy 2.4.0):

🕸️ Connections

Path: type hints ─▶ generics & variance ─▶ protocols ─▶ pydantic boundary

  • Used by dataclasses and pydantic: the libraries that read annotations at runtime on purpose.
  • Contrasts with runtime validation: static checks prove code, validation checks data.
  • Builds on dunder protocols: hints describe the shapes protocols and ABCs formalise.
  • Used by protocols: structural interfaces that only a checker enforces.
  • Same idea elsewhere: TypeScript's types are erased at runtime too, with the same "types prove code, not data" boundary.

notes.title: Generics & Variance
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Generics (typing spec) · 📜 PEP 695: type parameter syntax · 📜 PEP 612: ParamSpec · 📖 mypy docs: generics

⚡ TL;DR

A generic carries the type through (first(cats) is a Cat); Any throws it away. Read-only is covariant, write-only is contravariant, read-and-write is invariant: so accept Sequence, not list.

🧭 Flow: declare a type parameter def first[T](xs: Sequence[T]) -> T ─▶ the checker binds T from the argument ─▶ the result keeps that type ─▶ passing G[Cat] where G[Animal] is expected depends on how G uses T ─▶ only reads it: allowed ─▶ reads and writes it: rejected

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does a generic buy over Any? The type is carried through: first(cats) is Cat, still checked.
Why isn't list[Cat] a list[Animal]? Lists are mutable, so invariant: accepting it would allow inserting a non-Cat.
How do you keep a decorated function's signature? Type the decorator with ParamSpec: Callable[P, R] -> Callable[P, R].

💡 The idea

Typed loosely, a helper that works on any sequence forgets what's inside:

def first(xs: Sequence[Any]) -> Any:
    return xs[0]
first([1, 2]).upper()                # the checker allows this: Any switches checking off

Declare a type parameter and the return type is tied to the argument:

def first[T](xs: Sequence[T]) -> T:  # 3.12+ syntax; before, T = TypeVar("T")
    return xs[0]
reveal_type(first(cats))             # → Revealed type is "Cat"   (mypy 2.4.0)

Generics raise the variance question at once. A function taking list[Animal] can append(Animal()), so passing it a list[Cat] would let a plain Animal into your cats:

add_animal(cats)
# → error: Argument 1 to "add_animal" has incompatible type "list[Cat]"; expected "list[Animal]"
# → note: "list" is invariant ... Consider using "Sequence" instead, which is covariant

A read-only Sequence[Animal] parameter accepts list[Cat], because code that only reads can't insert the wrong thing.

The trade: generics keep type information across boundaries, and variance decides when a container of subtypes may stand in for the supertype, depending on whether it can be written to.

⚙️ How it works

Variance follows from what a type does with its parameter:

Contravariance is the reversed case. A Callable[[Animal], None] can be used where a Callable[[Cat], None] is expected, because a function that handles any animal handles every cat; mypy accepts it.

Variance of your own generics. With PEP 695 syntax (3.12+) the checker infers it from how the class uses T; with TypeVar you declare it (covariant=True). At runtime parameters are erased: isinstance([], list[int]) raises TypeError: isinstance() argument 2 cannot be a parameterized generic.

💻 Code

A generic repository and a signature-preserving decorator, the two places generics pay off most in service code:

import functools
from collections.abc import Callable, Sequence
from typing import Protocol

class HasId(Protocol):
    id: int

class Repo[T: HasId]:                          # bound: T must have an int `id`
    def __init__(self) -> None: self._rows: dict[int, T] = {}
    def add(self, row: T) -> None: self._rows[row.id] = row
    def get(self, row_id: int) -> T | None: return self._rows.get(row_id)

def summarise(items: Sequence[HasId]) -> list[int]:   # read-only, so it accepts list[User]
    return [i.id for i in items]

def timed[**P, R](fn: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]:   # ParamSpec: signature survives
    @functools.wraps(fn)
    def wrapper(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
        return fn(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

Repo[User]().get(1) is a User | None to every caller; timed keeps the exact parameter types instead of (*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: A generic ties types together across a boundary: def first[T](xs: Sequence[T]) -> T makes first(cats) a Cat, so checking continues downstream, while Any accepts everything and stops checking. On 3.12+ type parameters go inline, def f[T] and class Box[T], with bounds like [T: HasId]; before that, TypeVar and Generic. They're erased at runtime: generics exist for the checker.

Q · Mechanism — Why is list[Cat] not a list[Animal], but Sequence[Cat] is a Sequence[Animal]? A list is read and written: if accepted, the receiver could append(Animal()) and the owner, still holding a list[Cat], would later read a non-Cat. So list is invariant. Sequence exposes no writes, so the receiver can only read elements as animals, which every Cat is: covariant. It reverses for arguments: a function accepting any Animal can replace one that needs a Cat, so Callable parameters are contravariant. The API rule: accept the most permissive read-only type.

⚖️ Compare

Invariant Covariant Contravariant
Uses T by reading and writing producing (returning) consuming (arguments)
Examples list, dict, set Sequence, Iterator, tuple, frozenset, Mapping values Callable[[T], …] arguments
G[Cat] where G[Animal] expected ❌ ✅ ❌ (G[Animal] where G[Cat] expected ✅)

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Cat is an Animal, so list[Cat] is a list[Animal]"
    ✅ Mutable containers are invariant.
    ↳ Fix: accept Sequence[Animal] if you only read.
  • ❌ "Generic types are checked at runtime"
    ✅ They're erased: list[int] is just list, and isinstance(x, list[int]) raises TypeError.
  • 🔀 Not the same as Any
    ↳ Difference: a generic preserves the relationship between types; Any discards it.
  • ⚠️ Don't type read-only parameters as list or dict.
    ↳ Why: callers can't pass subtypes or other containers.
    ↳ Instead: Sequence, Mapping or Iterable.
  • ⚠️ Don't write decorators as Callable[..., Any].
    ↳ Why: every decorated function loses its signature.
    ↳ Instead: ParamSpec, as in the Code section.
  • 🔖 Version: TypeVar/Generic 3.5+; ParamSpec 3.10+; PEP 695 syntax 3.12+; type-parameter defaults 3.13+.
    ↳ Note: mypy results from mypy 2.4.0.

🕸️ Connections

Path: type hints ─▶ generics & variance ─▶ protocols

  • Builds on type hints: what the checker does with annotations.
  • Used by decorators: ParamSpec is how to type them without erasing signatures.
  • Used by protocols: generic protocols like SupportsRead[T].
  • Contrasts with Any: one function for many types, with the types kept instead of thrown away.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java's List<? extends Animal> (covariant) and List<? super Cat> (contravariant); Kotlin's out and in.

notes.title: Protocols & Structural Typing
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 typing.Protocol · 📘 Protocols (typing spec) · 📜 PEP 544: structural subtyping · 📖 mypy docs: protocols and structural subtyping

⚡ TL;DR

An ABC accepts what inherits from it; a Protocol accepts whatever fits its shape. The checker verifies the full shape; @runtime_checkable isinstance checks only that the member names exist.

🧭 Flow: declare class Closeable(Protocol) with method signatures ─▶ pass any object where it's expected ─▶ the checker compares every member's name and signature, no inheritance needed ─▶ mismatch: an error listing the conflicting members ─▶ at runtime, isinstance works only with @runtime_checkable, and checks names only

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Protocol vs ABC conformance? Structural, by matching members vs nominal, by subclassing or register.
What does the checker compare? Every member: names, parameter and return types, attribute types.
What does @runtime_checkable isinstance check? That an attribute with each member name exists: no signatures, not even callability.
isinstance on a plain Protocol? TypeError: only @runtime_checkable protocols allowed.
Why are protocols good for test doubles? A fake conforms by shape without importing or inheriting anything.
✏️ Draw by hand: structural vs nominal Protocol ⇠ vendor client, fake (dashed, no inheritance) · ABC ◁─ adapter (solid, inherits).

💡 The idea

Duck typing needs no declarations, def shutdown(r): r.close(), but nothing checks it until it runs. An ABC makes it checkable, but only for classes that subclass your base: a stdlib file or a vendor client is rejected even with exactly the right close. Declare the interface as a Protocol instead:

from typing import Protocol
class Closeable(Protocol):
    def close(self) -> None: ...
def shutdown(resource: Closeable) -> None:
    resource.close()
class File:
    def close(self) -> None: ...
class Sock:
    def close(self, force: bool) -> None: ...
shutdown(File())     # ✅ shape matches, no inheritance
shutdown(Sock())     # ❌ mypy 2.4.0: incompatible type "Sock"; expected "Closeable"
                     #    Expected: def close(self) -> None   Got: def close(self, force: bool) -> None

mypy compared the signatures, not just the name. Now add @runtime_checkable to a Serializer(Protocol) with def dumps(self, obj: object) -> bytes: a class whose dumps takes no argument passes isinstance, and so does a class with dumps = 5.

The trade: protocols let the checker verify duck typing by shape across code you don't own, and in exchange give up runtime enforcement: @runtime_checkable checks names, not signatures.

⚙️ How it works

Who conforms to what, structurally and nominally (the LLM-service seams from the Code section):

Dashed arrows need no import and no inheritance; the solid one is a real subclass that also inherits with_retries. Where each check happens (markers match Break it):

Rule What actually happens
Statically, conformance is complete Every declared member, with compatible types, under the normal variance rules: a method taking a wider argument or returning a narrower result still conforms. Protocols can be generic and combine by inheriting.
At runtime, names only @runtime_checkable makes isinstance check that each member name exists (via inspect.getattr_static on 3.12+); no signatures, return types or callability. It costs ~136 ns per call against ~18 ns for a concrete class (CPython 3.12).
Explicit subclassing still allowed Inheriting from a protocol declares intent and can supply defaults; it's then checked nominally too, but it's optional, and that's the point.

💻 Code

The pluggable seams of an LLM service, as protocols, so SDK clients, adapters and fakes all conform without inheriting:

from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from typing import Protocol

class ChatModel(Protocol):
    name: str
    async def complete(self, prompt: str, *, max_tokens: int) -> str: ...
    def stream(self, prompt: str, *, max_tokens: int) -> AsyncIterator[str]: ...

class Cache(Protocol):
    async def get(self, key: str) -> str | None: ...
    async def set(self, key: str, value: str, ttl_s: int) -> None: ...

async def answer(model: ChatModel, cache: Cache, prompt: str) -> str:
    if (hit := await cache.get(prompt)) is not None:
        return hit
    text = await model.complete(prompt, max_tokens=512)
    await cache.set(prompt, text, ttl_s=3600)
    return text

Conformance is checked where objects are used: a Redis cache, a dict wrapper and a no-op cache all fit, verified against the exact signatures including keyword-only max_tokens. No @runtime_checkable: dispatch is by configuration, not isinstance.

⚠️ Break it: a runtime check that looks like validation.

from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable
@runtime_checkable
class Serializer(Protocol):
    def dumps(self, obj: object) -> bytes: ...
class Broken:
    def dumps(self): return "oops"        # no argument, returns str
s = Broken()
if isinstance(s, Serializer):              # ① ② "only call it if it conforms"
    s.dumps({"a": 1})                      # ③
# look for: Broken PASSES isinstance, then the call fails
# naive model predicts: isinstance is False, so the call is skipped

On CPython 3.12 the check passed and the call raised TypeError: Broken.dumps() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given. The guard gave exactly the false confidence it was meant to prevent; mypy reports that Broken doesn't conform wherever it's used as a Serializer.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: A Protocol is an interface defined by shape: any type with compatible members conforms, whether or not it inherits. It's static duck typing, checked by mypy or pyright with full signatures. An ABC is nominal: you subclass or register, isinstance enforces it at runtime, and it can carry shared code. Protocols fit interfaces over code you don't own and test fakes; ABCs fit in-house hierarchies with shared behaviour.

Q · Mechanism — How does @runtime_checkable work, and what are its limits? Without it, isinstance against a protocol raises TypeError. With it, the protocol's metaclass checks that the object has an attribute for every member name, using getattr_static so properties aren't triggered. It doesn't check signatures, parameter counts, return types or even callability, and it's several times slower than a concrete isinstance. Use it for coarse routing, never as validation.

Q · Failure — A teammate dispatches on isinstance(obj, Serializer) and a malformed plugin blows up mid-request. What happened, and what's the design? The check only verified that an attribute named dumps existed (see Break it), so the request path called a wrong-signature method. For in-repo plugins, register through a typed function, register(s: Serializer), so the checker verifies the full signature in CI. For plugins loaded dynamically, check once at load time with a real call against a known input and fail startup, not per request.

Q · Design — An LLM gateway swaps providers, a cache and a vector store. Protocols or ABCs, and where does it break? Protocols for the seams (ChatModel, Embedder, VectorStore, Cache), because implementations come from vendor SDKs, adapters, local servers and fakes. An ABC for the in-house adapter layer when adapters share retries, metrics and token accounting: @abstractmethod blocks half-built adapters (the class diagram). It breaks on semantics: two providers can both conform yet differ in token counting, chunk boundaries and errors, so contract tests run against every adapter. I'd watch contract-test failures per provider first.

⚖️ Compare

Protocol ABC Plain duck typing
Conformance structural: has the members nominal: subclass or register none declared
Checked statically ✅ full signatures ✅ via inheritance ❌
Checked at runtime names only, with @runtime_checkable ✅ isinstance, instantiation blocked for missing abstracts ❌ until called
Classes you don't own ✅ only by register, unchecked ✅
Shared implementation if you subclass it ✅ the usual reason ❌

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "@runtime_checkable makes isinstance verify the protocol"
    ✅ It checks that member names exist (see Break it).
    ↳ Fix: rely on the checker; validate plugins once at load time.
  • 🪞 "To type an interface, implementations must inherit from it"
    ✅ With a Protocol, the checker matches by shape, so vendor classes and fakes conform as they are.
  • 🔀 Not the same as an ABC
    ↳ Difference: protocols are structural and mainly static; ABCs are nominal, runtime-enforced and carry shared code (ABCs).
  • 🔀 Not the same as no typing
    ↳ Difference: plain duck typing checks nothing until a call fails; a protocol is duck typing the checker verifies.
  • ⚠️ Don't design huge protocols.
    ↳ Why: every implementer must satisfy every member.
    ↳ Instead: small protocols, composed where needed.
  • ⚠️ Don't mix sync and async members by accident.
    ↳ Why: a sync method doesn't conform to an async def member.
  • 🔖 Version: Protocol 3.8+ (PEP 544); getattr_static in runtime checks 3.12+.
    ↳ Note: checked with CPython 3.12.13 and mypy 2.4.0.

🕸️ Connections

Path: generics & variance ─▶ protocols ─▶ ABCs & duck typing

  • Contrasts with ABCs: nominal and runtime-enforced, versus structural and checker-enforced.
  • Builds on dunder protocols: the language's own protocols (__iter__, __len__) were always structural.
  • Same mechanism as the iterator protocol: anything with the right methods works, ancestry irrelevant.
  • Used by test doubles and pluggable adapters: fakes and vendor clients fit the same seam.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Go interfaces and TypeScript's structural types are satisfied implicitly by shape, like protocols.

notes.title: ABCs & Duck Typing
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 abc: abstract base classes · 📘 collections.abc · 📘 Glossary: EAFP · 📖 GeeksforGeeks: abstract classes in Python

⚡ TL;DR

An ABC catches a missing method at construction, not at the call: ABCMeta checks __abstractmethods__. isinstance against an ABC can mean inherited, registered or shape-matched, and register() verifies nothing.

🧭 Flow: subclass an ABC ─▶ class creation records unimplemented @abstractmethods in __abstractmethods__ ─▶ instantiating with any left raises TypeError, at startup not at the call ─▶ isinstance(obj, ABC) checks real inheritance, then register(), then __subclasshook__

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
How does @abstractmethod prevent instantiation? ABCMeta records unimplemented abstracts; instantiation raises TypeError if any remain.
How does Iterable accept classes that never inherited it? __subclasshook__ checks for __iter__: shape, not ancestry.
What does register() check? Nothing: the class passes isinstance whether or not it implements anything.

💡 The idea

A plain base class with raise NotImplementedError lets a subclass that forgot a method be created; the mistake surfaces only when that method is finally called, perhaps in a nightly job. Make the base an ABC:

import abc
class Exporter(abc.ABC):
    @abc.abstractmethod
    def export(self, rows): ...
    @abc.abstractmethod
    def close(self): ...
class CsvExporter(Exporter):
    def export(self, rows): return "\n".join(map(str, rows))
CsvExporter()
# → TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class CsvExporter without an implementation for abstract method 'close'

Caught at construction (CPython 3.12). ABCs also do something surprising: isinstance(Rows(), Iterable) is True for a class that only defines __iter__, and after Exporter.register(Liar) an empty Liar passes isinstance(Liar(), Exporter) while hasattr(Liar(), "export") is False.

The trade: ABCs move "you forgot to implement this" from call time to construction time and let isinstance recognise interfaces, at the cost of a metaclass and a register() escape hatch that checks nothing.

⚙️ How it works

Three different ways to be a member of an ABC:

Only the solid arrow enforces abstract methods; both dashed ones make isinstance true without any check. The order isinstance tries them in, and the separate instantiation check:

abc.ABC's metaclass is ABCMeta (metaclasses): at class creation it collects every still-abstract method into __abstractmethods__ (here frozenset({'close'})), and object.__new__ refuses a class whose set isn't empty.

The idiom beside ABCs is EAFP: call the method and handle the exception, rather than checking first with isinstance or hasattr (LBYL), which works for any object that behaves and avoids check-then-act races.

💻 Code

An ABC that enforces the contract and carries shared behaviour, the case ABCs are for:

import abc, logging, time
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class ProviderAdapter(abc.ABC):
    max_attempts = 3

    def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str:              # template method: shared behaviour
        for attempt in range(1, self.max_attempts + 1):
            start = time.perf_counter()
            try:
                return self._call(prompt)
            except self.retryable_errors() as exc:
                log.warning("%s attempt %d: %s", type(self).__name__, attempt, exc)
            finally:
                record_latency(type(self).__name__, time.perf_counter() - start)
        raise RuntimeError(f"{type(self).__name__}: gave up")

    @abc.abstractmethod
    def _call(self, prompt: str) -> str: ...             # each provider implements
    @abc.abstractmethod
    def retryable_errors(self) -> tuple[type[Exception], ...]: ...

Every adapter gets identical retries and latency metrics, and one that forgets _call fails at startup. Callers can still type against a Protocol, so vendor clients fit without subclassing.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: @abstractmethod only flags a function; ABCMeta, the metaclass behind abc.ABC, records which abstract methods a class still hasn't overridden, and instantiating it raises TypeError. So a missing implementation is caught at construction, usually at startup, not when the method is eventually called. ABCMeta also customises isinstance, which is what makes register() and __subclasshook__ work.

Q · Mechanism — Explain register and __subclasshook__, and the danger they introduce. isinstance against an ABC accepts real subclasses, virtual subclasses added with register, and anything the ABC's __subclasshook__ approves, which is how Iterable recognises any class with __iter__ (the class diagram). The danger: register verifies nothing, and abstract-method enforcement doesn't apply to virtual subclasses, so isinstance against an ABC proves "declared", not "implemented": the same limit @runtime_checkable protocols have, reached another way.

⚖️ Compare

Plain base class abc.ABC Protocol
Missing method caught when called at instantiation by the static checker
isinstance recognises subclasses subclasses, registered, hook matches names only, with @runtime_checkable
Classes you don't own ❌ via register, unchecked ✅ structurally
Shared implementation ✅ ✅ possible, unusual
Best for nothing new in-house hierarchies with shared code interfaces across boundaries

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "isinstance(obj, SomeABC) means obj implements the interface"
    ✅ A registered class passes with no methods at all.
    ↳ So: it proves declared, not implemented.
  • ❌ "ABCs are Python's interfaces, so every abstraction should use one"
    ✅ A Protocol fits interfaces over code you don't own.
    ↳ Use an ABC for: construction-time enforcement plus shared behaviour.
  • 🔀 Not the same as a Protocol
    ↳ Difference: ABCs are nominal, runtime-enforced; protocols are structural, checker-enforced.
    ↳ So: good designs often use both: a protocol callers depend on, an ABC adapters inherit from.
  • ⚠️ Don't use register() to satisfy an isinstance check.
    ↳ Why: nothing is verified, so the failure moves to call time.
  • ⚠️ Don't write LBYL isinstance/hasattr checks by default.
    ↳ Instead: EAFP: call the method and handle the exception.
  • ⚠️ Don't add an ABC to a class another framework's metaclass also builds.
    ↳ Why: combining unrelated metaclasses raises a metaclass conflict (metaclasses).
  • 🔖 Version: abc.ABC 3.4+; the abstract-instantiation message was reworded in 3.12; collections.abc subscriptable for hints in 3.9.
    ↳ Note: checked on CPython 3.12.13 and 3.14.6.

🕸️ Connections

Path: protocols ─▶ ABCs & duck typing ─▶ runtime introspection

  • Builds on metaclasses: ABCMeta does all the work behind abc.ABC.
  • Contrasts with protocols: nominal and runtime versus structural and static.
  • Same mechanism as the iterator protocol: Iterable's hook recognises anything with __iter__.
  • Used by template-method designs: shared code in the base, required hooks as abstract methods.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java abstract classes, but Java has no register or shape-based isinstance.

notes.title: Runtime Introspection of Types
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 typing: introspection helpers · 📘 annotationlib (3.14)

⚡ TL;DR

Libraries turn hints into behaviour by reading them: get_type_hints resolves, get_origin/get_args walk, Annotated carries metadata. On 3.14 annotations are lazy: read them with annotationlib when names may not exist yet.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
get_type_hints vs __annotations__? Resolves string and forward references into real types; __annotations__ is raw.
get_origin / get_args of dict[str, int]? dict and (str, int).
What's Annotated for? Metadata checkers ignore and libraries read: Field(gt=0), FastAPI Query().

💡 The idea

Annotations are stored and ignored (type hints): a TypedDict is a plain dict, so Row(id="x", tags=1) builds {'id': 'x', 'tags': 1} without complaint. Libraries read hints on purpose, which is how pydantic, FastAPI and dataclasses turn one set of annotations into validation, serialisation and schemas: get_type_hints(obj, include_extras=True) resolves forward references, get_origin/get_args walk a type, and Annotated[int, …] metadata sits on .__metadata__. On 3.14, reading annotations can raise NameError for a name not yet defined; annotationlib.get_annotations(obj, format=Format.FORWARDREF) returns ForwardRefs instead. The cost: evaluation can fail, and it takes time at import.

💻 Code

from typing import Annotated, TypedDict, get_type_hints, get_origin, get_args
class Row(TypedDict):
    id: Annotated[int, "must be > 0"]
    tags: list[str]
h = get_type_hints(Row, include_extras=True)
print(get_origin(h["tags"]), get_args(h["tags"]), h["id"].__metadata__)
# → <class 'list'> (<class 'str'>,) ('must be > 0',)     (CPython 3.12)

notes.title: Pydantic v2 as a Validation Boundary
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Why use Pydantic · 📘 Validators · 📘 Strict mode · 📘 TypeAdapter · 📘 Serialization · 📘 Performance

⚡ TL;DR

Pydantic makes type hints true at runtime: untrusted data becomes a typed object, or a list of located errors. Build the validator once, parse raw bytes at the edge, and trust the types inside.

🧭 Flow: class defined ─▶ annotations + Field + validators become a core schema ─▶ pydantic-core (Rust) compiles a validator and a serializer, once ─▶ per request: raw bytes ─▶ model_validate_json parses and validates in one pass ─▶ typed instance, or one ValidationError holding every error ─▶ output through the separate serializer

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does Pydantic do that type hints don't? Checks and converts data at runtime against the annotations, and reports every error with its location.
Where should it sit? Where trust changes: HTTP, queues, config, third-party and LLM responses. Parse once, trust inward.
Lax vs strict? Lax coerces unambiguous values ("7" → 7); strict rejects the wrong type (int_type).
Why model_validate_json(bytes)? One Rust pass, no intermediate dict: 0.50 µs vs 1.25 µs for json.loads + model_validate.
Why build a TypeAdapter once? Building compiles the schema; per call it measured 4× slower (27 µs vs 6.8 µs).
✏️ Draw by hand: build once, run many Class ─▶ core schema ─▶ Rust validator + serializer (once); bytes ─▶ validator ─▶ instance or errors ─▶ serializer (per request).

💡 The idea

Python stores annotations and ignores them (see type hints). A checker proves the code consistent, but it never sees what arrives over the network. Pydantic reads the same annotations and checks the data:

from pydantic import BaseModel
class Transfer(BaseModel):
    amount: int
    to_account: str
Transfer.model_validate({"amount": "1000", "to_account": "acc_42"})
# → amount=1000 to_account='acc_42'     (the string was converted)
Transfer.model_validate({"amount": "ten"})
# → ValidationError: 2 errors: amount int_parsing, to_account missing

Two surprises sit in those lines. The first call converted a string, so "validated" doesn't mean "arrived as the declared type". The second reported both problems with their locations, not just the first. That's the shape of the whole library: "parse, don't validate". Convert untrusted input into a typed object at the edge once, then let the type carry the guarantee inward instead of repeated if checks.

The trade: you pay microseconds per payload at the edge and one declaration per shape, and in exchange the core never defends itself against malformed data again.

⚙️ How it works

Two phases, one expensive and done once, one cheap and done per request (markers match the Code section):

Rule What actually happens
Validator order mode="before" sees raw input (a str), type validation and coercion run, mode="after" sees the typed value (an int), then @model_validator(mode="after") sees the whole model: the place for cross-field rules.
Errors are collected Every field is checked before raising, so one ValidationError lists them all, each with a loc path like ('items', 0, 'qty').
Lax vs strict Lax suits query strings and forms, which are always strings. ConfigDict(strict=True) or Field(strict=True) rejects the wrong type outright. extra="forbid" rejects unknown keys; frozen=True blocks assignment (frozen_instance).
Serialization is its own schema model_dump uses the compiled serializer: Field(exclude=True) keeps a secret out of every response, serialization_alias="userId" emits camelCase. What you accept and what you emit can differ.
The escape hatch model_construct() skips validation entirely: it built LineItem(qty=-5) without complaint. Only for data you already validated.

💻 Code

A boundary module for an HTTP service: strict where types must be exact, bounded payloads, validators built once.

from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, TypeAdapter, ValidationError, model_validator

class LineItem(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True, extra="forbid", frozen=True)  # JSON body: exact types
    sku: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=64)]
    qty: Annotated[int, Field(gt=0, le=1_000)]

class CreateOrder(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", frozen=True)
    customer_id: int
    items: Annotated[list[LineItem], Field(min_length=1, max_length=200)]   # bound the payload

    @model_validator(mode="after")                     # cross-field rule: sees the whole model
    def unique_skus(self) -> "CreateOrder":
        if len({i.sku for i in self.items}) != len(self.items):
            raise ValueError("duplicate sku")
        return self

ITEM_LIST = TypeAdapter(list[LineItem])                # ① module level: schema built ONCE

def parse_create_order(raw: bytes) -> CreateOrder:
    try:
        return CreateOrder.model_validate_json(raw)    # ② parse + validate in one Rust pass
    except ValidationError as exc:                     # ③ every error, located → HTTP 400
        raise BadRequest(exc.errors(include_url=False)) from None

One bad request shows what each setting buys. Pydantic 2.13.5 returned three errors in one exception:

Input fragment loc type Setting that caught it
"coupon": "x" ('coupon',) extra_forbidden extra="forbid": a typo is an error, not ignored
"qty": 0 ('items', 0, 'qty') greater_than Field(gt=0)
"qty": "3" ('items', 1, 'qty') int_type strict=True on LineItem
two "sku": "a" () value_error the model validator (runs only once fields pass)

⚠️ Break it: lax mode at a service-to-service boundary.

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
class Transfer(BaseModel):
    amount: int
    to_account: str
class StrictTransfer(Transfer):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)
payload = {"amount": "1000", "to_account": "acc_42"}
print(Transfer.model_validate(payload))           # lax
try:
    StrictTransfer.model_validate(payload)        # strict
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e.errors()[0]["type"])
# look for: lax ACCEPTS "1000" as 1000; strict rejects it with int_type
# naive model predicts: both reject a string where an int is declared

It printed amount=1000 to_account='acc_42', then ValidationError int_type. Between services a string amount means the client serialised something wrong, and lax mode silently hides that bug. Choose strictness per boundary.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Pydantic reads annotations, Field constraints and validators when a model is defined, compiles them into a validator in its Rust core, and runs incoming data through it: the result is a typed instance or a ValidationError listing every problem and where it is. I put it where trust changes (HTTP bodies, queue messages, config, LLM and third-party responses), parse raw bytes with model_validate_json, and let the core trust the types. It's the runtime half of the type system.

Q · Mechanism — What happens between model_validate_json(raw) and an instance, and why beat json.loads + model_validate? The expensive work already happened at class definition: core schema built, validator and serializer compiled in Rust. model_validate_json hands the bytes to that validator, which parses incrementally and validates each value as it goes, so no intermediate dict of Python objects is allocated and then walked again. Measured on a 3-field payload: 0.50 µs, against 1.25 µs for json.loads + model_validate, and 0.85 µs for an unvalidated dataclass.

Q · Failure — p99 regressed after a refactor that moved parsing into a helper. No logic changed. What do you look for? Validator construction in the per-call path: TypeAdapter(list[Item]) inside the helper, a model class defined inside a function, or create_model() per request. Each recompiles the schema; a 20-item list went from 6.8 µs to 27 µs. Next: a switch from model_validate_json to json.loads + model_validate, the same data validated twice, model_dump then re-validate to "copy", or a before validator doing a regex compile or DB lookup per call. A sampling profiler shows core_schema building in the hot path.

Q · Design — Validation for an LLM gateway: untrusted HTTP in, provider responses back, tokens streamed out. Inbound, strict frozen extra="forbid" models with length limits and a raw-body cap, so bad requests are a 400 at the edge. Provider responses and tool-call arguments are validated before anything acts on them, and failures are non-retryable unless the provider allows a repair turn. Not on the per-token path: validating every chunk on the event loop across thousands of streams burns CPU, so tokens pass with a framing check and the assembled result is validated once. Separate input and output models. I'd watch the share of CPU spent in validation, and 400 rates by error type.

⚖️ Compare

BaseModel @dataclass TypedDict TypeAdapter
Runtime validation ✅ ❌ types never checked ❌ a plain dict ✅
Coercion lax default, strict opt-in ❌ ❌ same as models
Parses JSON directly ✅ model_validate_json ❌ ❌ ✅ validate_json
Output control aliases, excludes, computed asdict only it is a dict dump_python / dump_json
Best for boundaries: HTTP, config, LLM I/O internal value objects typing existing dicts lists, unions, non-model types

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "A model guarantees the input had exactly the declared types"
    ✅ Lax mode converts: "1000" became 1000 (see Break it).
    ↳ Fix: strict=True where the wire format should already be exact.
  • 🪞 "Use Pydantic for every class, for safety"
    ✅ Validation belongs at trust boundaries.
    ↳ Why: re-validating typed data inside the core costs CPU and adds nothing; dataclasses are the lighter tool there.
  • 🔀 Not the same as a dataclass
    ↳ Difference: both declare fields with annotations; a dataclass never checks a value, a model validates and converts every value at construction.
  • ⚠️ Don't build models or TypeAdapters per call.
    ↳ Why: each build recompiles the schema: 4× slower on a 20-item list.
    ↳ Instead: module level, built once at import.
  • ⚠️ Don't use one model for request and response.
    ↳ Why: it couples input and output shapes and leaks internal fields.
  • ⚠️ Don't call model_construct on untrusted data.
    ↳ Why: it bypasses every check.
  • 🔖 Version: this is Pydantic v2, whose Rust core replaced v1's pure-Python validation; v1 names (parse_obj, @validator, .dict()) are deprecated.
    ↳ Note: measured with Pydantic 2.13.5 on CPython 3.12.13 (arm64); the ratios transfer, not the microseconds.

🕸️ Connections

Path: type hints ─▶ runtime introspection ─▶ Pydantic ─▶ structured outputs

  • Builds on runtime introspection: Pydantic resolves annotations at runtime to build its schema.
  • Used by structured outputs: the same models generate JSON Schema for LLMs and validate their replies.
  • Contrasts with dataclasses: same field declarations, no runtime checks.
  • Used by reliability mechanics: a ValidationError is non-retryable; a transport error may be retried.
  • Same idea elsewhere: FastAPI builds request parsing, response models and OpenAPI from these models; Zod plays this role in TypeScript.

notes.title: Structured Outputs & Tool Schemas
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Pydantic: JSON Schema · 📘 OpenAI: Structured model outputs · 📘 Claude: Structured outputs · 📘 Pydantic: Validators

⚡ TL;DR

One Pydantic model is the contract: it becomes the schema the LLM must fill, and it validates what comes back. Strict mode guarantees the shape of the output, never that the values make sense.

🧭 Flow: Pydantic model ─▶ model_json_schema() ─▶ translate to the provider's strict subset (+ CI contract test) ─▶ provider compiles a grammar, cached ─▶ constrained decoding masks invalid tokens ─▶ response JSON ─▶ model_validate_json with the same model ─▶ act, or repair once

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
JSON mode vs structured outputs? JSON mode: valid JSON syntax. Structured outputs: conformance to your schema, via constrained decoding.
How is conformance enforced? The provider compiles the schema to a grammar and masks invalid tokens at each decoding step.
Why can a valid Pydantic model be rejected? Providers accept a subset: e.g. OpenAI wants every property in required, and a default makes a field optional.
Why validate a constrained response? Unsupported constraints were stripped, and schema-valid values can still be wrong.
What does each tool schema cost? Prompt tokens on every request, plus grammar compilation the first time.
✏️ Draw by hand: the round trip Lanes App · Provider: model ─▶ schema ─▶ translate ─▶ grammar ─▶ masked decoding ─▶ JSON ─▶ same model validates.

💡 The idea

The oldest approach describes the format in the prompt and hopes:

text = call_llm("Return JSON with keys query (string) and limit (integer or null).")
# '```json\n{"query": "gpus", "limit": "ten"}\n```'
json.loads(text)   # → JSONDecodeError: the code fence. Next time: a missing brace, an invented key

Failures arrive per request, at random. Structured outputs replace hope with a mechanism: define the shape once as a Pydantic model, send its JSON Schema, and the provider constrains decoding so tokens that would break the schema can't be generated.

But the schema the provider sees isn't your class. It's generated JSON Schema, and each provider accepts only a subset of it. A model that validates perfectly in tests can be rejected at the provider, or accepted and filled with values that are well-typed and wrong: picture a form where the clerk can't write outside the boxes, but can write nonsense inside them.

The trade: structured outputs turn "does it parse?" from a per-request gamble into a guarantee, and in exchange your schemas are limited to each provider's subset, and the values still need checking.

⚙️ How it works

The round trip starts and ends in the same model (① and ③ match the Code section; ② happens at the provider):

Rule What actually happens
Three levels of guarantee Prompt-and-parse: nothing. JSON mode: syntax only, it parses. Structured outputs and strict tools: schema conformance, because the grammar makes invalid output impossible within the supported subset.
The schema is part of the prompt Field names and Field(description=…) are what the model reads; constraints like ge become minimum. Every tool schema is resent on every request, so wide schemas cost tokens each call.
Provider subsets differ As read on 22 Sep 2026: OpenAI wants every property required (optional = type | null), additionalProperties: false, a root object, ≤5,000 properties, ≤10 levels. Anthropic also wants additionalProperties: false, has no minimum/maximum or string lengths, no recursive schemas, and caps a request at 20 strict tools, 24 optional and 16 union parameters; grammars are cached 24 h.
Why you still validate Stripped constraints aren't enforced by the decoder (limit can come back -3), and a well-formed ID can refer to nothing. The same model restores every constraint.

💻 Code

One model as the source of truth: translate it for the provider, validate the response with it.

import copy
from pydantic import BaseModel

UNSUPPORTED = ("default", "title", "minimum", "maximum", "maxItems", "minLength", "maxLength")

def to_strict_schema(model: type[BaseModel]) -> dict:             # ① translate for the provider
    """Constraints removed here are re-enforced when the response is validated."""
    schema = copy.deepcopy(model.model_json_schema())
    def clean(node: dict) -> None:
        for key in UNSUPPORTED:
            node.pop(key, None)
        if node.get("type") == "object" and "properties" in node:
            node["required"] = list(node["properties"])         # every key present
            node["additionalProperties"] = False
            for sub in node["properties"].values():             # recurse into property SCHEMAS,
                clean(sub)                                      # never into the name mapping
        for key in ("items", "anyOf", "allOf", "$defs"):
            child = node.get(key)
            if isinstance(child, dict):
                clean(child) if key == "items" else [clean(c) for c in child.values()]
            elif isinstance(child, list):
                for c in child:
                    clean(c)
    clean(schema)
    return schema

def parse_tool_args(model: type[BaseModel], raw_json: str) -> BaseModel:
    return model.model_validate_json(raw_json)                  # ③ restores ge / le / lengths

The recursion goes into property schemas, never the properties mapping: an early version popped every key named title and silently deleted a model field called title. Run on a Search model with a nested Filter(title=…), Pydantic 2.13.5 kept title, moved $defs objects to all-required with additionalProperties: false, and parse_tool_args rejected "limit": -3 with greater_than_equal, a constraint the provider never saw.

⚠️ Break it: two fields that look equally optional.

from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
class SearchArgs(BaseModel):
    query: str
    limit: int | None = Field(description="Max results, or null")   # nullable, no default
    page: int | None = None                                          # nullable WITH a default
    sort: Literal["relevance", "date"] = "relevance"                 # plain default
schema = SearchArgs.model_json_schema()
print("properties:", list(schema["properties"]))
print("required:  ", schema["required"])
# look for: page and sort are NOT required: they have defaults
# naive model predicts: page is as required as limit, since both are int | None

It printed properties: ['query', 'limit', 'page', 'sort'] and required: ['query', 'limit']. Only the default decides required, so page is rejected by a provider that demands every property be required and counts against a cap on optional ones. Use X | None with no default and apply defaults in code.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: In a Python stack the tool schema comes from a Pydantic model: model_json_schema() turns fields, descriptions and constraints into JSON Schema, translated to the provider's strict subset. The provider compiles it into a grammar and constrains decoding, so the output always matches the shape. Then I validate the response with the same model, which restores constraints the provider dropped. Strict mode guarantees shape; correctness is still my job.

Q · Mechanism — Three ways to get structured data out of an LLM: what does each guarantee? Prompt-and-parse guarantees nothing: code fences, missing keys, wrong types, random per request. JSON mode guarantees json.loads succeeds, but keys and types are still the model's choice. Structured outputs (response_format on OpenAI; output_config.format and strict: true tools on Anthropic) compile the schema into a grammar that masks the token distribution, so conformance is guaranteed within the subset. None guarantees meaning, so the response is validated and side-effecting calls get business checks.

Q · Failure — The agent works in dev and fails in prod with schema-rejection errors. The model's code is unchanged. What happened? The generated schema or the provider's rules changed. Usual triggers: a field gained a default (dropped from required, see Break it), a union pushed past Anthropic's 16 union parameters, a new ge or max_length emitted a keyword the subset rejects, a recursive model, or a Pydantic upgrade changed the output. Dump the exact translated schema prod sends and diff it with dev's. Structurally: one translation function, plus contract and snapshot tests in CI per tool per provider.

Q · Design — A tool-calling layer for an agent with 30 tools: correct, bounded in cost, safe to change. A registry of (name, description, args model, handler); schemas generated through the translation, snapshot-tested so changes review like API diffs, and contract-tested against each provider. Arguments come back through the original model, and side-effecting handlers check business rules first. Thirty schemas resent per request cost tokens and exceed Anthropic's 20 strict tools, so select a handful per turn by route, state or retrieval. Version tools like APIs: never repurpose a field name. I'd watch schema rejections by tool, local validation failures by field, and tool-definition tokens per request.

⚖️ Compare

Prompt and parse JSON mode Structured outputs / strict tools
Syntax guaranteed ❌ ✅ ✅
Keys and types guaranteed ❌ ❌ ✅ within the supported subset
Meaning guaranteed ❌ ❌ ❌ validate + business rules
Fails randomly, per request wrong keys or types, per request schema rejected at deploy
First-use cost none none grammar compilation, then cached

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "With structured outputs I don't need to validate"
    ✅ The decoder enforces only the supported subset.
    ↳ Proof: limit: -3 was schema-valid once minimum was stripped, and failed local validation.
  • 🪞 "int | None and int | None = None give the same schema"
    ✅ The default removes the field from required (see Break it).
  • 🔀 Not the same as JSON mode
    ↳ Difference: JSON mode guarantees parseable JSON; structured outputs guarantee your schema, via constrained decoding.
  • 🔀 Not the same as correctness
    ↳ Difference: conformance (right keys and types) is the provider's job; correctness (right values) is yours: validation, business rules, evals.
  • ⚠️ Don't send every tool on every request.
    ↳ Why: schemas cost tokens each call and hit per-request limits.
    ↳ Instead: select a relevant subset per turn.
  • ⚠️ Don't hand-write provider schemas.
    ↳ Why: they drift from the model that validates the response.
  • 🔖 Version: provider rules as read 22 Sep 2026; Anthropic's GA renamed output_format to output_config.format.
    ↳ Note: Pydantic 2.13.5 emits JSON Schema draft 2020-12 with $defs; contract tests, not this note, are the source of truth.

🕸️ Connections

Path: type hints ─▶ Pydantic ─▶ structured outputs ─▶ reliability mechanics

  • Builds on Pydantic: the model, its schema and response validation.
  • Builds on type hints: X | None versus a default decides required.
  • Used by reliability mechanics: the repair turn is a bounded retry; a validation error isn't retried blindly.
  • Used by testing: schema snapshot tests and provider contract tests in CI.
  • Same idea elsewhere: FastAPI publishes OpenAPI from the same model_json_schema() machinery; Instructor and PydanticAI wrap this loop.
